title: How do you decide between optimizing for latency vs throughput?
summary: Probes whether you understand these are often in tension, not both maximizable, and can pick correctly for a stated use case.

slides.markdown:
This question probes whether "make it faster" means one thing to you or two. **Latency** is how long one request takes; **throughput** is how many requests the system handles per second. They're often in tension — the moves that raise one can lower the other.

By the end of this topic you'll have a decision rule: name the SLA that actually matters for this workload, then optimize for that one, instead of treating "performance" as a single undifferentiated goal.

The first thing to pin down: is this a **user-facing request path** (a page load, a search query) or a **background/batch job** (a nightly report, a data pipeline)? The two have almost opposite priorities.

A user is waiting on the first; nobody's watching a live clock on the second. That single distinction usually tells you which metric — p99 latency or requests/sec — actually matters here, before you touch any architecture.

slides.sectionTitle: The answer skeleton: name the SLA, then optimize for it
slides.markdown:
The reliable skeleton: **name the SLA that matters for this specific workload, then optimize for that one metric** — not for "performance" in the abstract.

A checkout page has a latency SLA (respond in under 300ms or users bounce); a log-ingestion pipeline has a throughput SLA (process 1M events/sec, individual delay barely matters). Stating which SLA governs this system, out loud, is the move that turns a vague question into a concrete design decision.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: batching raises throughput, hurts tail latency
slides.markdown:
**Batching** — waiting to collect several requests before processing them together — is the clearest example of the tension. A queue that waits 50ms to batch 100 writes into one database call raises throughput (fewer round trips, less per-item overhead) but adds up to 50ms of latency to *every* item in that batch, even the first one that arrived.

The first request in the batch pays the full wait even though it was ready instantly — that's the concrete cost throughput gains are bought with.

**Request coalescing** merges identical concurrent requests (say, 50 clients asking for the same uncached product page at once) into a single backend call, with the result fanned back out to all 50 callers. Throughput wins — one backend hit instead of 50 — but the 49 callers who arrived after the first now wait for a request they didn't make.

It's a good trade when the requests are truly identical and cheap to fan out; it's a bad one if any caller needed a slightly different, per-user answer.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: connection pooling helps both, at once
slides.markdown:
Not every optimization is a trade-off — **connection pooling** (reusing a warm set of database connections instead of opening a new one per request) cuts per-request latency (no handshake cost) *and* raises throughput (the database handles more requests/sec without connection-setup overhead eating cycles).

It's worth naming this kind of move explicitly: interviewers want to see that you know the trade-off isn't universal, only that some techniques genuinely sit on it.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: the same path, optimized for latency vs throughput
slides.markdown:
![Two versions of the same client to queue to worker path: one optimized for latency processing each request immediately, one optimized for throughput batching requests before processing](assets/latency-vs-throughput.svg)

Same components, different queueing discipline — process-immediately minimizes the wait per item; batch-then-process minimizes total work per item, at the cost of every item waiting for the batch to fill.

slides.sectionTitle: The trade-off to name out loud: p50 vs p99 move opposite ways
slides.markdown:
| | Batch size 1 (no batching) | Larger batch |
|---|---|---|
| p50 latency | Low — processed immediately | Higher — waits to fill batch |
| p99 latency | Low — no batch wait tail | Can spike — worst-case wait for a slow-to-fill batch |
| Throughput | Lower — more per-item overhead | Higher — overhead amortized across the batch |
| Resource efficiency | Lower | Higher |

**How to decide:** if p99 latency is the SLA, keep batches small or skip batching; if throughput per dollar is the SLA, batch aggressively and accept the latency tail.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: what if both matter equally?
slides.markdown:
If the interviewer says both latency and throughput matter equally, the honest move is to **segment the traffic** rather than pick one global setting. Real-time requests (a live checkout) get the low-latency path — small or no batching, dedicated capacity. Background requests (a receipt email) get the high-throughput path — aggressive batching, shared capacity.

One-size-fits-all optimization is usually the tell that a candidate hasn't internalized that these are different SLAs, not one dial.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: how do you measure which one you're winning on?
slides.markdown:
Name the actual metrics, not "it feels faster." For latency: **p50, p95, and p99** response times — p99 specifically, since averages hide the tail that angry users actually experience. For throughput: **requests/sec** or **items processed/sec** sustained under load, not a burst peak.

Tracking both side by side over time, per change, is how you catch a batching tweak that quietly doubled throughput while tripling p99 — a regression an average would hide entirely.

**Wrong belief:** "Faster" is a single thing you optimize for, and any optimization moves you toward it.

**Why it's wrong:** a change that raises throughput (bigger batches, more concurrency) can simultaneously make individual requests slower — the two aren't the same axis, and a candidate who conflates them will propose a fix that quietly regresses the metric that actually mattered.

**Correct model:** always name which of the two you're optimizing for, and check the other one didn't silently get worse as a result.

If you only have a minute: name whether this is a user-facing path (optimize p99 latency) or a batch/background job (optimize throughput), then pick techniques that match — small batches and dedicated capacity for the former, aggressive batching and shared capacity for the latter.

Call out any technique, like connection pooling, that actually helps both — and always measure p50/p95/p99 alongside requests/sec so a throughput win can't hide a latency regression. See [latency vs throughput](latency-vs-throughput) for the underlying vocabulary.
